questions.prompt: Which of the following correctly describes the real difference between a security engineer's job and a security architect's job, per Lesson 1?
options: An engineer implements and operates a specific control correctly within one system; an architect decides which controls should exist in the first place and how they fit together across the organization
An architect is simply a more senior title for the exact same day-to-day configuration work an engineer does
An engineer designs the multi-year architecture roadmap, while an architect implements the individual firewall rules and IAM policies
The two roles are distinguished only by pay grade, not by any real difference in scope or time horizon
questions.explain: An engineer's question is 'how do I implement this control correctly, on this system, right now' — scoped to one system, days-to-weeks horizon. An architect's question is a layer up: which controls should exist, how they fit together, and what's being traded away — a multi-year horizon, formalized by both the NIST NICE Workforce Framework and the CISSP CBK as genuinely distinct disciplines.
questions.distractorExplain: Option C reverses the actual roles entirely — it's the architect who produces the multi-year roadmap and architecture decision records, while the engineer produces the working configuration and closed ticket. Swapping which role does the designing and which does the implementing is exactly the confusion this lesson is built to prevent.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of the 2013 Target breach, as described in Lesson 3, in the correct order.
items: Attackers obtain credentials belonging to a third-party HVAC vendor
Attackers use that access to enter a vendor-management segment of the network
Attackers move from the vendor segment into systems handling point-of-sale and cardholder data
The breach succeeds because segmentation between the vendor-facing function and the payment environment wasn't real
questions.explain: The breach is a segmentation failure, not a missing-patch story: stolen vendor credentials provided entry into a vendor-management segment, and from there attackers reached the payment-card environment specifically because the segmentation between those two business functions didn't actually isolate them from each other — exactly the pattern enterprise-scale defense in depth has to design against.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: when a control's cost genuinely exceeds its benefit, the architecturally correct move is to document a risk ________ naming the gap, the residual risk, and the accountable owner who signs off — rather than silently skipping the control.
questions.explain: A documented risk acceptance — what the gap is, why it's being left open, what the residual risk is, and who is signing off on carrying it — is what separates a deliberate, defensible tradeoff from an undocumented gap that surfaces during an audit or an incident.

questions.prompt: Which of the following correctly defines SABSA, per Lesson 5?
options: Sherwood Applied Business Security Architecture — a practitioner-built, business-driven security architecture framework organized into six layers, each traceable back to a named business attribute
The Open Group Architecture Framework's security-specific module, organized around four domains abbreviated BDAT
CISA's five-pillar, four-stage model for assessing zero trust maturity across an organization's technology architecture
An international standard certifying an organization's Information Security Management System through accredited audit
questions.explain: SABSA was created by John Sherwood, Andrew Clark, and David Lynas — three working security architects, not a standards committee — and its defining rule is traceability: every control, down through its six layers from Contextual to Operational, has to justify itself against a named business attribute.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B describes TOGAF, a different framework covered in the very next lesson — TOGAF organizes around the four BDAT domains (Business, Data, Application, Technology) and treats security as a cross-cutting concern rather than having SABSA's six-layer, business-traceable structure. Confusing TOGAF's process-oriented domains with SABSA's content-oriented layers is exactly the mix-up this chapter is built to prevent.

questions.prompt: Security isn't one of TOGAF's four BDAT domains. Per Lesson 6, what does that actually mean in practice?
options: Security is a cross-cutting concern addressed inside every ADM phase, from A through H, rather than confined to one dedicated domain
Security has no defined place anywhere in the TOGAF methodology and must be handled entirely outside the ADM
Security is only ever reviewed once, during Phase D, and never touches any other phase
TOGAF requires security architecture to be designed before Phase A begins, outside the ADM cycle entirely
questions.explain: The Open Group's own guidance, most notably the TOGAF Series Guide on Integrating Risk and Security, treats security as a cross-cutting concern addressed inside every ADM phase — vision, business architecture, information systems, technology architecture, solutions, migration planning, and implementation governance — rather than confined to a single dedicated domain the way Business, Data, Application, and Technology are.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about using CISA's Zero Trust Maturity Model as an architecture input, per Lesson 7.
options: A ZTMM baseline scores five pillars against four maturity stages: Traditional, Initial, Advanced, and Optimal
Gaps between a pillar's current and target maturity stage become candidate work packages in TOGAF's Phase E
A pillar already sitting near Optimal gets deprioritized in sequencing rather than re-litigated
A ZTMM assessment by itself tells an architect exactly which specific products to buy
An architect using ZTMM this way starts by picking controls, then checks maturity afterward to confirm the choice
questions.explain: Used as an architecture input, ZTMM produces a scored baseline across five pillars against four maturity stages, and the gaps between current and target stage become candidate work packages that Phase E and F sequence rationally — pillars furthest from target or most exposed go first, and a pillar already near Optimal is deprioritized. The whole point of using it this way is that the architect starts by assessing where the organization actually is, not by picking controls first and checking maturity as an afterthought.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a common blending pattern uses TOGAF as the outer ________ and SABSA as the inner content, with the ADM supplying cadence and governance while SABSA supplies business-traceable substance.
questions.explain: Because TOGAF is a process framework (how an enterprise architecture practice runs) and SABSA is a content framework (what the security architecture should contain), the two are frequently paired: TOGAF's ADM cycles govern cadence and governance while SABSA's layers and Business Attributes Profile fill in the security substance inside phases A through D.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 9, why does scoring risk with Likelihood x Impact 'flatten a distribution into one number' in a way that actually misleads a risk committee?
options: Two risks that average to the same score can have wildly different tail outcomes — a tight, predictable medium-impact risk isn't the same business problem as a rare, catastrophic one, even if a 5x5 matrix scores them identically
The matrix always underestimates likelihood and always overestimates impact, in every single case
Multiplying two numbers together is mathematically invalid for any risk scoring purpose
A 5x5 matrix can only ever be used for financial risk, never for cybersecurity risk
questions.explain: Real-world loss isn't one outcome, it's a range — a ransomware event might cost $50,000 if caught early or $8 million if it hits backups. 'Impact = 4' erases that entire range, so two risks that happen to average to the same score can have completely different tail risk, which is exactly why mature programs eventually reach for quantitative methods like FAIR that model a range of loss instead of a single point score.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the FAIR model, per Lesson 11.
options: FAIR decomposes Loss Event Frequency into Threat Event Frequency multiplied by Vulnerability
FAIR decomposes Loss Magnitude into Primary Loss and Secondary Loss
FAIR typically runs estimated ranges through a Monte Carlo-style simulation rather than a single-point multiplication
FAIR is an informal, in-house spreadsheet trick with no published standard behind it
Organizations typically run full FAIR analysis on all 200 items in a risk register's backlog
questions.explain: FAIR is a formal, published model maintained by the FAIR Institute (also published as The Open Group's O-RA standard), decomposing Loss Event Frequency into Threat Event Frequency times Vulnerability, and Loss Magnitude into Primary and Secondary Loss, with ranges run through Monte Carlo simulation to produce a distribution rather than a point score. It's reserved for the handful of risks that justify that effort, not run across an entire 200-item backlog — that's what qualitative scoring is for.

questions.prompt: Match each risk treatment option from Lesson 12 to what it actually commits an organization to.
right: Eliminating the activity or exposure that creates the risk entirely, rather than reducing it
A documented decision to take no further action because the cost of treating the risk exceeds the benefit
Shifting the financial consequence of a risk to another party via insurance or contract, without eliminating it
Reducing likelihood, impact, or both by implementing a control
questions.explain: ISO 31000's four treatment options each commit the organization to something different: accept means a documented decision to do nothing further, mitigate means reducing likelihood or impact with a control, transfer means shifting who pays via insurance or contract without removing the underlying risk, and avoid means eliminating the exposure entirely rather than reducing it.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: ISO 31000 defines risk as 'the effect of ________ on objectives.'
questions.explain: ISO 31000's deliberately abstract definition — the effect of uncertainty on objectives — has to cover financial, safety, and project risk, not just cybersecurity, which is why most security teams operationalize it into the Likelihood x Impact shorthand for day-to-day triage.

questions.prompt: Three separate teams each maintain their own tracking sheet for the same firewall rule control, and the control owner fields three separate audits of it in one quarter. Per Lesson 13, what does a real GRC program do instead?
options: Treats governance, risk, and compliance as three views onto the same underlying set of controls — assess the control once and map it to every framework it satisfies
Assigns the control to whichever of the three teams has the most available capacity that quarter
Eliminates two of the three disciplines entirely, since governance, risk, and compliance are ultimately redundant with each other
Requires the control owner to produce a fourth, consolidated tracking sheet summarizing the other three
questions.explain: The failure mode GRC exists to prevent is exactly this: three teams, three sheets, the same control re-audited three times with nothing getting safer, just more exhausting. A real GRC program assesses one control once, maps it to every framework it satisfies at the same time, and governs its ownership and exception path through one documented accountability structure.

questions.prompt: Put these elements of the security documentation hierarchy from Lesson 14 in order from most abstract to most concrete.
items: Policy — states what the organization requires and why, approved at the executive or board level
Standard — translates the policy into specific, measurable requirements
Procedure — the exact step-by-step sequence a person or script follows to meet the standard
questions.explain: Policy sets the what-and-why at a level abstract enough to survive a change of vendor or technology; a standard translates that into specific, testable requirements; a procedure is the literal click-by-click how-to. Conflating these levels — a policy written at procedure-level detail, or a standard written at policy-level vagueness — is what causes real governance problems, not just stylistic ones.

questions.prompt: Match each GRC tooling category from Lesson 15 to what it actually does.
right: A crosswalk showing which requirement in each framework a given control satisfies, assessed once and reapplied automatically
A centralized system of record for risk registers, control libraries, and policy across a large organization, such as RSA Archer
Connects via API to cloud and SaaS tools to continuously pull audit evidence instead of gathering it manually, such as Vanta
Distributes policy documents, collects signatures, and tracks who hasn't acknowledged the current version
questions.explain: Platform GRC suites like RSA Archer or ServiceNow GRC centralize risk registers and control libraries for large organizations. Automated evidence platforms like Vanta connect via API to continuously pull evidence instead of manual screenshot-gathering. Attestation platforms handle distribution, signature collection, and tracking of policy acknowledgment. Control-to-framework mapping is the crosswalk that lets one assessed control show as satisfied across every framework it maps to.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: something that almost went wrong but didn't — like someone noticing a suspicious email before clicking it — is called a ________, and it's the highest-value signal a GRC program can collect.
questions.explain: A near-miss shows a control working at the exact moment of human judgment, for free, before anything became a real incident. An organization where near-misses get reported constantly and openly is one where people trust that reporting won't be held against them — rare near-miss reports usually mean people have learned not to say anything, not that nothing is going wrong.

questions.prompt: An enterprise customer doing serious vendor due diligence asks a SaaS vendor for a SOC 2 Type II report rather than a Type I. Per Lesson 17, why?
options: Type II tests operating effectiveness with sampled evidence across a review period, while Type I only tests whether controls were suitably designed as of a single point in time
Type I is more expensive to produce, so Type II is simply the cheaper option customers prefer
Type I and Type II test identical evidence; the only difference is which Trust Services Criteria are in scope
Type II is a certificate, while Type I is only a self-reported attestation with no CPA firm involved
questions.explain: A Type I report answers whether controls would achieve their objective if they operated as described — a design claim, as of one date. A Type II report tests whether those same controls actually operated that way over a review period, typically six to twelve months, with sampled evidence like access-review logs and termination records. A control designed well on June 1st but not consistently followed by October tells a buyer almost nothing if all they have is Type I.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about ISO 27001's Statement of Applicability (SoA), per Lesson 18.
options: For every Annex A control, the SoA records whether it's applicable, implemented, or not applicable with a documented justification
Annex A is a catalog an organization draws from based on its own risk assessment, not a mandatory checklist to implement in full
A vague or missing justification for an excluded Annex A control is a real red flag in due diligence
The bare ISO 27001 certificate is considered more informative to a due-diligence reviewer than the SoA itself
Every organization must implement all 93 Annex A controls regardless of its own risk profile
questions.explain: The SoA is what makes an organization's control selection explicit and auditable — applicable/implemented or excluded-with-justification, for every Annex A control. Annex A itself is a catalog to draw from based on risk, not a mandatory checklist, so a legitimate exclusion needs a real justification; a vague one is exactly the kind of red flag a careful reviewer should ask about. That's also why anyone evaluating a vendor's certification should ask to see the SoA itself, not just the certificate.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: under PCI DSS, the people, processes, and technology that store, process, or transmit cardholder data — the thing that defines assessment scope — is called the Cardholder Data ________.
questions.explain: The Cardholder Data Environment is the single most consequential concept in a PCI DSS assessment — a huge amount of practical compliance work is actually scope reduction, isolating systems that truly need to touch card data and routing everything else through a validated third-party processor so the organization's own systems never see raw card numbers.

questions.prompt: Put these stages of the ISO 27001 certification process, per Lesson 18, in the correct order.
items: Stage 1 audit — the certification body reviews ISMS documentation and readiness
Stage 2 audit — the certification body tests whether the ISMS is actually implemented and operating
Surveillance audits — typically annual, smaller-scope audits confirming the ISMS still functions
Recertification audit — a full reassessment, typically every three years
questions.explain: ISO 27001 certification isn't a one-time event: Stage 1 checks documentation readiness, Stage 2 tests whether the ISMS is genuinely operating (and results in certification if successful), annual surveillance audits confirm it's still functioning between full reassessments, and a full recertification audit runs roughly every three years — a cadence that reflects a genuinely sustained program rather than a one-time push.

questions.prompt: A vendor answers every question on a SIG questionnaire perfectly but can't produce a SOC 2 report or any audit evidence when asked. Per Lesson 22, what should the assessing organization conclude?
options: That gap is itself a finding worth escalating — a questionnaire response is a self-attestation, and the highest-risk tiers need independent evidence to corroborate it
Nothing further is needed; a perfect questionnaire score is sufficient evidence on its own for any vendor tier
The vendor should automatically be placed in the lowest-risk tier, since it was cooperative in answering the questionnaire
The questionnaire itself must be flawed if a vendor can score perfectly without supporting evidence
questions.explain: A questionnaire response is the vendor grading its own homework. A mature assessment process backs the highest-risk tiers with independent evidence — a current SOC 2 Type II report, an ISO 27001 certificate and SoA, a recent pentest summary. A vendor that answers perfectly but can't produce any of that when asked is itself a finding worth escalating, not a clean pass.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about vendor risk management, per Lessons 21, 23, and 24.
options: Outsourcing a function to a vendor never outsources the accountability that goes with it
A right-to-audit clause exists in most vendor contracts but is rarely exercised as a literal on-site audit against large cloud providers
A vendor's clean intake assessment has an effective expiration date, because staff, infrastructure, and ownership all change over time
A Business Associate Agreement transfers HIPAA regulatory accountability away from the covered entity entirely
Fourth-party risk only matters if the organization holds a direct contract with the fourth party
questions.explain: If a vendor mishandles your data or becomes an attacker's entry point, the incident is still yours — regulators, customers, and boards hold the organization accountable regardless of a BAA or contract, which only allocates cost and liability after the fact, never regulatory accountability itself. Right-to-audit clauses exist as leverage and a fallback right, rarely exercised literally against hyperscale providers. And a vendor's security posture changes continuously, which is exactly why intake assessments have an effective expiration date. Fourth-party risk matters precisely because there's no direct contract or visibility into it at all.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: risk introduced by a vendor's own subcontractors and suppliers, one layer removed from direct visibility, is called ________-party risk.
questions.explain: Your cloud provider's own subcontractors, your payroll vendor's background-check processor, your SaaS provider's underlying cloud infrastructure — each is a fourth party you have no direct contract with, no direct visibility into, and often no idea exists, but whose failure can still reach you through your vendor.

questions.prompt: Match each vendor-risk term from Lessons 22-23 to what it actually is.
right: A contractually defined window, commonly 24-72 hours, for a vendor to notify the customer of a security incident
A comprehensive, modular vendor questionnaire maintained by Shared Assessments
Contract language giving the customer the right to audit a vendor's relevant security controls with reasonable notice
A questionnaire built for cloud service providers, mapped to the Cloud Security Alliance's Cloud Controls Matrix
questions.explain: SIG is Shared Assessments' comprehensive, reusable vendor questionnaire. CAIQ is the Cloud Security Alliance's cloud-specific version, mapped to its Cloud Controls Matrix. A right-to-audit clause gives the customer a contractual hook to verify controls directly. A breach notification timeline turns 'notify us promptly' into an enforceable, concrete window, commonly 24-72 hours.

questions.prompt: Which of the following correctly describes a metric that would pass all three of Lesson 25's tests for belonging on a board report?
options: Percent reduction in critical unpatched systems, trended quarter over quarter against a board-approved target
Number of alerts triaged this quarter
Total CVSS score summed across every currently open finding
Number of security tools currently deployed across the environment
Hours spent by the SOC team on incident response this month
questions.explain: Percent reduction in critical unpatched systems, trended against a target, is inherently a trend (not a single snapshot), maps directly to a risk the board already owns (exploitation of known vulnerabilities), and points toward a decision (approve more remediation budget, or confirm the trend is on track).
questions.distractorExplain: Option B, 'number of alerts triaged,' is the textbook activity-count failure: it says the team was busy, not whether risk went up or down, it maps to no specific enterprise risk category, and it implies no decision at all — exactly the kind of metric that lands with a shrug in a boardroom despite being a perfectly reasonable thing to track on an engineering dashboard.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 26's translation chain, what should the 'business consequence' stage actually express, given a technical finding like an unpatched critical RCE vulnerability?
options: What the realistic threat scenario actually costs the business in categories executives already track — lost revenue, regulatory exposure, contractual penalties, reputational damage, and recovery cost
The exact CVSS score and its exploitability, attack complexity, and privilege-required sub-scores
A restatement of the technical finding using simpler, non-technical vocabulary for the same facts
A qualitative High/Medium/Low label with no further detail, since executives don't need more than that
questions.explain: The translation chain moves from technical finding, to threat scenario, to business consequence, to dollar range. The business-consequence stage is specifically where the finding gets converted into categories a CFO, general counsel, or board member already tracks — lost revenue, regulatory exposure, contractual penalties, reputational damage, recovery cost — none of which requires anyone to know what CVSS even stands for.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the SEC's cybersecurity disclosure rules and related obligations, per Lesson 28.
options: Form 8-K Item 1.05 requires disclosure within four business days of the materiality determination, not of the incident's discovery
Materiality is a legal judgment made jointly by the CISO, legal and privacy counsel, and typically a disclosure committee — never by the security team alone
State data-breach notification laws and SEC materiality-based disclosure are two separate, parallel obligations triggered by different tests
GDPR's 72-hour notification requirement is the same obligation as the SEC's four-business-day disclosure rule, just under a different name
The SEC's four-business-day clock starts running at the moment the incident is first discovered
questions.explain: The four-business-day clock runs from the materiality determination, not discovery — which is exactly why having a disclosure committee ready in advance matters. Materiality is a securities-law judgment made jointly by legal, privacy counsel, the CISO, and typically a disclosure committee. Breach notification laws protect individuals and trigger on exposure of their data; SEC disclosure protects investors and triggers on materiality — two separate obligations on different clocks, which is why GDPR's 72-hour rule and the SEC's four-business-day rule are not the same requirement.

questions.prompt: Match each element of a real board security report from Lesson 27 to its purpose.
right: The specific decision, budget approval, or risk acceptance the report requests
Three to five metrics shown as a trend line against a target, not a point-in-time number
Quantified exposure using FAIR so the board can weigh risks against other enterprise priorities
One or two sentences stating whether risk is improving, stable, or worsening overall
questions.explain: The headline posture is the single most important line, opening with an overall judgment. Trended metrics give the board context over time rather than an isolated number. Top risks in dollar ranges, quantified with FAIR, let the board weigh cyber risk against every other enterprise risk competing for the same capital. The ask is what turns the report into a governance input rather than a status update — boards notice when it's missing.

questions.prompt: In the Meridian Specialty Lending lab, tokenizing cardholder data at intake is prioritized over a point solution that satisfies only one business attribute. Per Lesson 29, why?
options: It shrinks the PCI DSS cardholder-data environment to a small, auditable boundary, lowering both audit cost (Regulatory standing) and ongoing security spend (Cost discipline) at the same time
It is the cheapest single control available, regardless of how many business attributes it happens to serve
It eliminates the need for any network segmentation elsewhere in Meridian's architecture
It is the only control in the design that satisfies Meridian's Operational resilience attribute
questions.explain: Tokenization removes raw card numbers from everything downstream of the intake point, which shrinks the Cardholder Data Environment to a small, auditable boundary — the single biggest lever Meridian has over both audit cost and ongoing security spend at once. That's exactly the kind of decision Lesson 29's conceptual strategy step prioritizes: controls that satisfy more than one business attribute over point solutions that satisfy only one.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the Northfield Processing case study, per Lesson 31.
options: Both the SOC 2 Type II audit and the ISO 27001 certification were accurate, given exactly what each was scoped to test
The legacy administrative API wasn't in either audit's sample population because it was never in the IAM team's asset inventory in the first place
The static API key used by the compromised third-party vendor had never been rotated since it was set up
The breach happened because the independent audit firms were negligent or missed evidence they should have caught
Compliance checking is meant to be an exhaustive discovery process that finds every asset and access path in an organization
questions.explain: Both audits sampled correctly within their defined scope and reported honestly — the real gap sat one layer up, in Northfield's own asset inventory, which never captured the legacy administrative API because it only tracked human user accounts, not service-to-service integrations. The API's static key had never been rotated since setup. The lesson explicitly isn't that the auditors were negligent; a compliance audit tests the control environment as the organization itself has bounded it, and was never designed to be an exhaustive discovery process on its own.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 31, compliance checking verifies a defined set of controls against a defined scope — it is a ________, not a ceiling.
questions.explain: Compliance is a necessary, genuinely hard-won baseline — a floor — but it was never designed to be an exhaustive discovery process that finds every asset and access path across an organization. That's the job of continuous asset discovery and periodic architecture review, looking at the whole system the way an architect does, not just the parts a specific audit's scope statement happened to name.
